name: Edward VI

died.cause: A lung disease, probably tuberculosis, at age 15

summary: Son of Henry VIII and Jane Seymour who became king at nine; under his regents England moved from Henry's Catholic-style church without the pope to a fully Protestant one, with the Book of Common Prayer, until his early death brought his Catholic half-sister Mary I to the throne.

key_dates.label: Becomes king at nine (28 January); his uncle Edward Seymour rules as Lord Protector; royal injunctions order images removed and chantries dissolved
First Book of Common Prayer replaces the Latin Mass (Whitsunday, 9 June); clergy allowed to marry; Prayer Book Rebellion in Devon and Cornwall
New ordinal for ordaining clergy; stone altars ordered replaced by wooden tables; Joan Bocher burned for heresy
Dispute with his half-sister Mary over her private Mass; her chaplains arrested
Second, more Protestant Book of Common Prayer; the Duke of Somerset executed (22 January)
Forty-two Articles issued; his 'Device for the Succession' names Lady Jane Grey as heir; dies 6 July

accomplishments.text: His reign was the second swing in England's religious changes: Henry VIII had broken with Rome but kept Catholic worship; under Edward the English church became fully Protestant; under Mary I it returned to Rome; under Elizabeth I it became Protestant again.

Under his regents Archbishop Thomas Cranmer replaced the Latin Mass with the English Book of Common Prayer (1549, revised in a more Protestant direction in 1552), allowed priests to marry, and issued the Forty-two Articles (1553), the basis of the later Thirty-nine Articles.

In parish churches images, shrines, and wall paintings were removed or whitewashed, chantries that paid priests to pray for the dead were dissolved and their property seized, and stone altars were replaced by communion tables.
Was educated as a convinced Protestant, and his journal and letters show him taking a personal interest in religious reform.

Welcomed Continental Protestant refugees, including Martin Bucer and Peter Martyr Vermigli, who were made professors at Cambridge and Oxford, and allowed a church for foreign Protestants in London (1550).
Conservative bishops who resisted the changes, including Stephen Gardiner of Winchester and Edmund Bonner of London, were deprived of their sees and imprisoned.

Tried, as he was dying, to stop his Catholic half-sister Mary from succeeding by naming his Protestant cousin Lady Jane Grey in his 'Device for the Succession'; Jane reigned nine days before Mary took the throne.

victims_intro: Executions in the king's name during his minority. Edward was a child, so the decisions were largely those of his regents and council, though he signed some warrants himself.

victims.name: Joan Bocher
victims.condemned_by: Archbishop Cranmer's commission for heresy; the king's council
victims.allegation: Burned as an Anabaptist for denying that Christ took flesh from the Virgin Mary; a later story in Foxe that Edward signed her warrant in tears at Cranmer's urging is doubted by historians.
victims.verification_note: The execution is documented; Edward's personal role rests on a later, doubtful anecdote.

victims.name: George van Parris
victims.condemned_by: Commission for heresy under Archbishop Cranmer
victims.allegation: A Flemish surgeon burned for denying the divinity of Christ.
victims.verification_note: Executed under Edward's government; the king's own involvement is not recorded.

victims.name: Robert Welsh
victims.executed: Hanged from the tower of his church, St Thomas's, Exeter, 1549
victims.condemned_by: Royal commanders after the Prayer Book Rebellion
victims.allegation: A Catholic priest executed for his part in the rebellion against the 1549 Prayer Book.
victims.verification_note: Executed by royal forces; a decision of the commanders in the field rather than the king.

victims.name: Humphrey Arundell
victims.executed: Hanged, drawn, and quartered at Tyburn, January 1550
victims.condemned_by: Trial for treason under Edward's government
victims.allegation: Leader of the Cornish and Devon rebels of 1549 who demanded the return of the Latin Mass.
victims.verification_note: Executed for treason in the king's name.

persecution_note: Edward himself was never persecuted. His government put down the 1549 Prayer Book Rebellion with great force: royal troops under Lord Russell and Lord Grey, including foreign mercenaries, killed several thousand rebels in Devon and Cornwall.
excommunication_note: No pope excommunicated Edward by name. His realm was already outside the Catholic Church after Henry VIII's break with Rome, and Mary I reconciled it to Rome after his death.
